texto:
Field service management (FSM) is the discipline, and increasingly the software, used to organise work that happens at a customer's location rather than in a shop or over the phone. A boiler repair, a broadband installation, a lift inspection and a pest treatment all share the same problem: a request must become a scheduled job, a qualified technician must reach the right address with the right parts, and the visit must end in a record, an invoice and a payment. FSM systems manage that chain. They exist because every hour a technician spends driving or waiting is an hour that cannot be billed.
Gartner describes FSM as "a discrete market within the broader customer service and support software market", serving providers whose technicians travel to install, repair and maintain equipment, often under service or maintenance contracts. Microsoft used a similar framing in July 2015, calling it the part of customer service that handles end-to-end work performed at customer locations when a problem cannot be resolved by phone.
How the job moves through the system
The unit of work is the work order. It typically carries a customer and site record, a job type, a priority, a time window, required skills or certifications, expected duration, parts, and links to any equipment already installed at the address. In the residential trades, the order often begins as a phone call taken by a customer service representative (CSR), who books it into an open slot. In enterprise settings it may be generated automatically, from a contract renewal, a preventive maintenance calendar or a sensor alert.
Scheduling comes next. Simple tools present a calendar; more advanced engines treat the day as an optimisation problem, weighing technician skills, location, availability, travel time and service-level commitments. Salesforce, when it launched Field Service Lightning on March 15, 2016, described automated scheduling "based on skills, availability, and location", using optimisation technology from ClickSoftware.
Dispatch assigns and sequences jobs on a board that a dispatcher watches throughout the day, reshuffling when a job overruns or an emergency arrives. The technician receives the order on a mobile app, which records arrival and departure times, photos, checklists, signatures, parts used and upsell quotes. GPS location from the van or phone feeds both the dispatch board and arrival notifications sent to the customer.
The cycle closes with invoicing and payment, often taken on site, and with an updated asset history for the next visit. In the trades, vendors such as ServiceTitan, Jobber and Housecall Pro bundle these steps with estimates, consumer financing, membership plans and marketing tools. Enterprise suites from IFS, PTC's ServiceMax, Salesforce, Microsoft and Oracle lean further into asset management, contracts, inventory and parts logistics.
Operators sit on both sides of the transaction. On the business side, owners, CSRs, dispatchers and technicians use the system daily. On the demand side, lead sources (search ads, directories, marketplaces, call-answering services) increasingly plug into it, because a lead that cannot become a booked job has limited value.
From pagers to platforms
Field force automation predates the software category's current names. In 2006, Telstra told investors it had improved the efficiency of roughly 7,000 field technicians by fitting vehicles with GPS and field force automation systems from US company @Road, according to iTWire.
The enterprise market consolidated through the 2010s. Microsoft said on July 16, 2015 that it was acquiring FieldOne, a provider built on Dynamics CRM offering work order management, automated scheduling and mobile collaboration. Salesforce shipped Field Service Lightning in March 2016, starting at $135 for organisations with at least one Enterprise or Unlimited Service Cloud licence, according to the company. It went on to buy ClickSoftware, its scheduling partner, for $1.35 billion in 2019. GE Digital acquired ServiceMax in 2016 for $915 million and sold a 90% stake to Silver Lake in December 2018, according to diginomica. PTC agreed to buy ServiceMax for approximately $1.46 billion on November 17, 2022, and completed the deal on January 4, 2023. Gartner's 2022 Magic Quadrant for FSM named IFS a Leader for the seventh consecutive time.
A separate, faster-growing segment emerged for small and mid-sized trade contractors. Jobber launched in 2011 in Edmonton, according to chief executive Sam Pillar. ServiceTitan was founded in 2012. Housecall Pro was founded in 2013 and now says it serves more than 45,000 home service businesses, although an FAQ on the same page gives "over 40,000". ServiceTitan priced its initial public offering at $71 per share on December 11, 2024, raising $624.8 million, and began trading on Nasdaq as TTAN the next day.
Scale in this segment is measured partly by money flowing through the software. ServiceTitan reported gross transaction volume of $26.8 billion for the quarter ending July 31, 2026, up 17% year on year, on revenue of $292.8 million. Jobber said in 2023 that its customers delivered $13 billion of services to 27 million North American households in 2022.
Why it matters to marketers
For home service advertisers, FSM software is where advertising results are actually counted. A plumber's search campaign can record a call, but only the job record shows whether that call became a booked visit, a $150 repair or a $12,000 system replacement. Connecting the two is the central measurement problem for local lead generation.
Google built that connection into its own product. On December 7, 2020, ServiceTitan announced that customers could book jobs directly with Google Guaranteed contractors through Local Services Ads, with those bookings appearing in ServiceTitan; contractors could receive booking leads only through a partner platform. When Google merged the booking systems of Business Profiles and Local Services Ads in August 2024, Jobber and ServiceTitan were the first named integrations. Google's current partner directory also lists Housecall Pro and Workiz.
Outside Google, the same plumbing powers call tracking and AI answering. Invoca's home services product, released October 6, 2026, books, reschedules and cancels appointments through ServiceTitan and Salesforce Field Service and logs qualification data there. Yelp's planned $270 million purchase of Hatch brought a lead-response tool whose integrations span ServiceTitan and Jobber.
Feeding job revenue back into ad platforms is a second link. Advertisers typically export booked or completed jobs from FSM software as offline conversions for bidding. That route is narrowing: Google stopped accepting new adopters of offline conversion imports through the Google Ads API from June 15, 2026, pointing them to the Data Manager API, and its attribution models skip offline conversions uploaded more than seven days after the event.
Limits and disputes
Data quality is the most common weakness. Attribution is only as good as the CSR who tags the lead source, the technician who closes the job and the integration that passes both back. Duplicate customers, unlinked calls and jobs booked outside the system all break the chain.
Surveillance of workers is a long-running dispute. When Telstra rolled out vehicle GPS in 2006, Colin Cooper of the Communications, Electrical and Plumbing Union said employees were withholding consent and that "there needs to be agreement about proper safeguards to protect privacy", according to iTWire. Location tracking now sits in most technician apps.
Platform dependence cuts both ways. Booking integrations can lock contractors into a small set of approved vendors, and switching costs rise once customer histories, memberships and payments live in one system. Pricing for full suites is rarely published.
Market sizing varies widely. IMARC put the global FSM market at $6.6 billion in 2025, forecast to reach $19.9 billion by 2034. Global Market Insights estimated $5.49 billion for 2025 and $23.61 billion by 2035. Definitions, not just methods, differ between such reports.
Answering capacity has become an advertising cost. Invoca's benchmarks found people answered 52% of home services calls, and Google began billing unanswered Local Services Ads calls held for more than 20 seconds from October 1, 2026.
Not the same as
- Customer relationship management. CRM software stores customer and prospect records, interactions and sales opportunities. FSM handles what happens after a job is sold: scheduling, dispatch, on-site work and billing. Many vendors sell both.
- Workforce management. Workforce management usually refers to staffing, rostering and time tracking for employees in general, including call centres. FSM focuses on jobs at customer sites and the travel between them.
- Service-area business. A service-area business is a Google Business Profile category for companies that travel to customers with their address hidden. Many such businesses run FSM software, but the term describes a listing, not a system.
- Finite-state machine. In computing, FSM also abbreviates finite-state machine, a model of a system that moves between a fixed set of states.
Recent developments
Software vendors are rebuilding FSM around AI agents and AI-driven demand. At its Pantheon conference on October 6, 2026, ServiceTitan made its Max package of agents generally available to residential contractors and introduced Homh, a platform intended to make contractors discoverable and bookable by homeowners and their AI assistants, including ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, with confirmed appointments written directly into ServiceTitan.
Lead sources are moving the same way. Hatch, now part of Yelp, says its voice agents read technician availability, service areas and scheduling rules before turning calls into booked jobs. Google, meanwhile, is moving Local Services Ads into Google Ads in phases from August 2026, with accounts using booking configurations scheduled for a later wave. Its AI-qualified call conversions, introduced April 21, 2026, judge calls by recorded intent rather than duration alone. Booking decisions are moving upstream, while the FSM record remains where a job is confirmed as real.

Summary
Who: Trade contractors, utilities, telecoms and equipment makers use FSM; vendors include ServiceTitan, Jobber, Housecall Pro, IFS, PTC's ServiceMax, Salesforce and Microsoft; ad platforms and call-tracking firms such as Google, Yelp and Invoca integrate with it.
What: Software and practice for turning service requests into scheduled, dispatched, completed and invoiced jobs carried out at customer sites.
When: Field force automation was in commercial use by 2006; the enterprise market consolidated between 2015 and 2023, and trades platforms grew from 2011, with ServiceTitan listing in December 2024.
Where: Homes, businesses and industrial sites served by mobile technicians, with the strongest advertising links in North American home services.
Why: Travelling labour is costly to coordinate, and for local advertisers the FSM record is where a lead is proven to become revenue.
